result:
The town’s only clockmaker retired on a Tuesday, leaving a handwritten sign in the window:

**TIME WILL CONTINUE WITHOUT MY ASSISTANCE.**

Most people found this reassuring.

For forty-three years, he had repaired the clocks they brought him: kitchen clocks with greasy faces, wristwatches that had survived wars but not washing machines, a grandfather clock whose owner insisted it ran slowly whenever her brother visited.

“Perhaps,” the clockmaker had suggested, “your brother stays too long.”

Now he spent his mornings beside the river. Without a shop to open, he discovered that nine o’clock was less an event than a suggestion.

One afternoon, a girl approached carrying a small red alarm clock.

“You’re retired,” she said.

“Yes.”

“So you don’t have to fix this.”

“Correct.”

She set it on the bench between them.

“It belonged to my dad. It doesn’t work.”

The clockmaker looked at the river. A duck was struggling to swallow something it had badly overestimated.

“I haven’t brought my tools,” he said.

“I can come tomorrow.”

He turned the clock over in his hands. One screw was missing. The winding key was bent, and someone had scratched a tiny star into the paint beside the alarm switch.

“Was he a punctual man?”

“No,” she said. “We used to set it early.”

He tried the key, gently.

“Ten minutes?”

“Twenty. He knew about the ten.”

The clockmaker smiled.

“Tomorrow, then.”

That evening, he returned to the shop and packed a few tools into a canvas bag. Before leaving, he took down the sign.

On the back, he wrote:

**RETIRED.  
OCCASIONALLY AVAILABLE.**

He stood outside for a moment to check that it could be read through the glass, then went home before he could change his mind.
